## Results

We screened public human RNA-seq libraries for papillomavirus reads under three discovery strategies (Methods): an unbiased prevalence sweep of skin and related tissues (`r comma(stats$n_screened)` libraries screened), a targeted query of productive cutaneous lesions providing positive controls (`r stats$n_targeted` wart/epidermodysplasia-verruciformis skin libraries), and a broadened skin-neoplasia sweep capturing cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC), actinic keratosis (AK) and Bowen disease (`r comma(stats$n_csc)` libraries screened). Throughout, every screened library, including HPV-negative ones, was scored as papillomavirus reads per million (RPM) so that infection burden could be separated from sequencing depth, and each sample was annotated as primary tissue, cell line, or engineered material.

### HPV signal in public RNA-seq is dominated by cell-line and engineered artefacts

In the unbiased sweep, HPV positivity was strongly concentrated in non-primary material. Engineered libraries were HPV-positive in `r f2(stats$eng_pct)`% of cases (95% CI `r pci(stats$eng_lo, stats$eng_hi)`) and cell-line libraries in `r f2(stats$cl_pct)`% (`r pci(stats$cl_lo, stats$cl_hi)`), versus only `r f2(stats$clin_pct)`% (`r pci(stats$clin_lo, stats$clin_hi)`) of clinical primary-tissue libraries (@tbl-positivity). In logistic regression this corresponded to roughly five-fold higher odds of positivity for engineered (OR `r fo(stats$eng_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$eng_or_lo, stats$eng_or_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$eng_or_p)`) and cell-line (OR `r fo(stats$cl_or)`, `r oci(stats$cl_or_lo, stats$cl_or_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$cl_or_p)`) samples relative to clinical tissue (likelihood-ratio *P* = `r fp(stats$lr_p)`). These positives were almost entirely the high-risk mucosal alpha types: HPV18 accounted for `r stats$hpv18_cl`/`r stats$hpv18_tot` of its calls in cell lines and HPV16 for `r stats$hpv16_cl`/`r stats$hpv16_tot` (@supptbl-types), the expected signature of integrated-HPV cell lines such as HeLa and of their well-documented cross-contamination of archived sequencing data. Genuine primary skin therefore carries HPV at a low rate (2–4%, below), and the apparent abundance of HPV in public transcriptomes is largely a laboratory artefact that must be partitioned out before any prevalence claim.

The transcripts themselves carry an independent signature of that artefact, in two forms. E1 and E2 are encoded on the same early polycistronic message, so their read counts should track one another; integration characteristically disrupts the E2 open reading frame while sparing E1, inverting the ratio. Cell-line libraries show a median E1:E2 of `r fo(stats$e1e2_cl)`, against `r formatC(stats$e1e2_ctrl, format="f", digits=2)` in productive controls, `r formatC(stats$e1e2_skin, format="f", digits=2)` in unselected skin and `r formatC(stats$e1e2_neo, format="f", digits=2)` in neoplasia, and the ratio separates cell lines from productive primary infection almost completely (AUC 0.97, Wilcoxon *P* = 2.8×10⁻¹⁴; @fig-integration A). Where integration has gone further and the early region is lost but for E6 and E7, both E1 and E2 fall silent and no ratio can be formed; those libraries instead show oncogene transcription with no late transcription at all, the canonical integrated-carcinoma pattern, and are captured by that criterion. Together the two signatures call `r pp(stats$e1e2_cl_pct)`% of `r stats$e1e2_cl_n` cell-line libraries as integration-like (`r stats$e1e2_cl_ratio` by the inverted ratio, `r stats$e1e2_cl_e67` by the E6/E7-only pattern the ratio cannot see) while calling `r pp(stats$e1e2_ev_pct)`% of EV biopsies and `r pp(stats$e1e2_per_pct)`% of peri-lesional mucosa, the two tiers where infection is episomal by definition. That it reports integration rather than culture is settled by the one cell line in the cohort that maintains its genome episomally, an HPV31-positive HaCaT derivative, which sits at 0.6–1.0 alongside primary tissue rather than with the integrated lines. Applied as a detector, the ratio flags `r stats$e1e2_disc` libraries that carry the integration signature without being labelled as cell lines, including melanoma lines under shRNA knockdown recorded with a tissue source of "skin" and cutaneous SCC lines recorded with a carcinoma diagnosis, which is what motivates the engineered tier above. The ratio was checked against the event it claims to report. Calling virus–host chimeric reads against a combined human/HPV index in `r stats$jx_n` libraries spanning the range of the ratio separates the same groups completely (@fig-integration B), provided integration is scored as a *recurrent* junction rather than a raw count: the fraction of a library's junctions falling at its single most-supported site is `r stats$jx_int_range` where the ratio indicates integration and `r stats$jx_epi_range` where it does not, with no overlap. Raw counts are misleading in the opposite direction, since the two epidermodysplasia-verruciformis libraries generate the largest number of junctions in the panel while being episomal. The positive controls recover the expected answer unprompted: `r stats$jx_cl_int` of `r stats$jx_cl_n` cell-line libraries are integration-positive, and two independently return the same junction at chromosome 8q24, the documented integration site of the HeLa lineage.

The ratio was then read against a progression in which the answer is known independently. A cervical series (SRP252916) sequenced HPV16-positive normal epithelium, high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion and squamous carcinoma, six cases per arm under one rRNA-depleted protocol, alongside six HPV-negative normal controls; the arms are the submitting study's, and the tissue and the progression are ones the marker was not developed on. The HPV-negative controls returned no HPV of any type, and across the three positive arms the median E1:E2 rises monotonically with grade, from `r formatC(stats$cxg_norm, format="f", digits=2)` in normal epithelium (*n* = `r stats$cxg_norm_n`) through `r formatC(stats$cxg_hsil, format="f", digits=2)` in HSIL (*n* = `r stats$cxg_hsil_n`) to `r formatC(stats$cxg_scc, format="f", digits=2)` in carcinoma (*n* = `r stats$cxg_scc_n`), a shift of roughly eightfold in the direction integration predicts (@fig-integration C). Late transcription tracks the same axis without being part of the criterion: the libraries called episomal carry abundant L1, while those with a disrupted ratio carry almost none. The binary call is the weaker readout at this size, separating the carcinoma and lesion arms from normal epithelium (`r stats$cxg_scc_int` and `r stats$cxg_hsil_int` of six against `r stats$cxg_norm_int` of `r stats$cxg_norm_n`) but not from each other, and the normal-epithelium arm is thin: two of its six libraries yielded no HPV reads and a third carried two. The gradient, not the threshold, is what this series supports.

![Integration read from transcription, and confirmed against the event itself. (**A**) Distribution of the E1:E2 transcript ratio by population tier, as log~2~((E1 + 0.5)/(E2 + 0.5)) for libraries with at least five combined E1 and E2 reads. E1 and E2 are encoded on the same early message, so their counts track one another unless integration disrupts the E2 open reading frame; the dashed line at zero is parity. In-vitro material (cell lines, engineered cells) sits far above parity, primary tissue at or below it, and the episomal HPV31-positive HaCaT derivative falls with primary tissue rather than with the integrated lines. HPV-positive calls (Kraken2 ≥10 papillomavirus reads) among `r comma(stats$n_screened)` human RNA-seq libraries from the unbiased skin-and-related-tissue sweep, stratified by sample provenance. Cell-line and engineered libraries carry roughly five-fold higher odds of HPV positivity than primary tissue, and their positive calls are predominantly the integrated mucosal types HPV16 and HPV18, the expected signature of cell-line contamination. {#tbl-positivity}

### Skin neoplasia carries only trace HPV, not productive infection, and this is not a depth artefact

The central question, whether HPV is transcriptionally active in cSCC/AK or present only as a residual footprint, was resolved by the depth-normalised burden analysis (@fig-rpm). Productive controls (warts/condyloma) were detected at or above the control-calibrated detection floor (`r p1(stats$floor_rpm)` RPM) in `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of libraries, with a median burden of `r comma(stats$ctrl_medrpm)` RPM; the EV biopsy tier, sequenced most deeply of all (median `r mreads(stats$ev_medreads)` reads), reached it in `r pp(stats$ev_pctfloor)`% (median `r p1(stats$ev_medrpm)` RPM). In stark contrast, the neoplasia tier reached this floor in only `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`% of libraries (median `r formatC(stats$neo_medrpm, format="f", digits=3)` RPM), six orders of magnitude below the productive controls, despite being sequenced almost four times more deeply than they were (median `r mreads(stats$neo_medreads)` vs `r mreads(stats$ctrl_medreads)` reads). Unselected skin, once the peri-lesional and EV material that the targeted queries had swept into it was reassigned to its own tiers (Methods), forms an almost clean null: `r pp(stats$uns_pctfloor)`% of `r comma(stats$uns_n)` libraries reach the floor.

![Depth-normalised HPV transcript burden distinguishes productive warts, EV and peri-lesional mucosa from a trace-level signal in skin neoplasia and unselected skin. Each point is one Kraken2-screened RNA-seq library, scored as papillomavirus reads per million (RPM: Papillomaviridae clade reads ÷ (unclassified + root reads) × 10⁶) and grouped by population tier: unselected skin (*n* = `r comma(stats$uns_n)`), cell lines (`r comma(stats$cl2_n)`), engineered cells (shRNA/siRNA knockdowns and transgenes, in-vitro material regardless of its disease label; `r comma(stats$engt_n)`), productive controls (warts/condyloma; `r stats$ctrl_n`), epidermodysplasia verruciformis biopsies (EV; `r stats$ev_n`), cutaneous neoplasia (cSCC/actinic keratosis; `r stats$neo_n`), peri-lesional mucosa (condyloma-adjacent tissue; `r stats$per_n`), non-permissive tissue (cutaneous adipose, which has no stratified squamous compartment in which a papillomavirus could replicate; `r stats$npt_n`), and libraries with no recorded site (`r comma(stats$oth_n)`; the residual tier, 99% of which carries no site keyword in its SRA metadata rather than an identified non-cutaneous site). Points are jittered horizontally; boxes show the median and interquartile range; the *y*-axis is log~10~-scaled (RPM + 0.05). The dashed red line marks the control-calibrated detection floor (`r p1(stats$floor_rpm)` RPM, the 5th percentile of productive-control libraries). Productive controls lie far above the floor (median `r comma(stats$ctrl_medrpm)` RPM; `r pp(stats$ctrl_pctfloor)`% of libraries above floor), as do EV biopsies (`r pp(stats$ev_pctfloor)`%) and peri-lesional mucosa (`r pp(stats$per_pctfloor)`%), whereas neoplasia and unselected skin sit near zero (`r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor)`% and `r pp(stats$uns_pctfloor)`% above floor) despite neoplasia being sequenced far more deeply than the productive controls (median `r mreads(stats$neo_medreads)` vs `r mreads(stats$ctrl_medreads)` reads). Tier assignment is by metadata precedence with curated corrections (Methods): EV *cultures* (immortalised keratinocyte EV models) remain in the cell-line tier, whereas the EV tier holds the `r stats$ev_n` EV patient skin biopsies.](figure1.png){#fig-rpm}

This gap is not explained by sequencing depth. Modelling productive-level detection (RPM ≥ floor) as a function of population tier and log sequencing depth, productive controls exceeded unselected skin by close to four orders of magnitude (Fisher exact OR `r fo(stats$fish_or)`, 95% CI `r fo(stats$fish_lo)` to `r fo(stats$fish_hi)` under separation, *P* = `r fp(stats$fish_p)`), while neoplasia sat an order of magnitude above skin (OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$m2b_lo, stats$m2b_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p)`). That contrast is easier to read on the absolute scale from which the odds ratios derive: `r stats$ctrl_pos_floor`/`r stats$ctrl_n` productive controls cross the floor, against `r stats$neo_pos_floor`/`r comma(stats$neo_n)` neoplasia libraries and `r stats$uns_pos_floor`/`r comma(stats$uns_n)` skin libraries. Neoplasia is thus measurably, but marginally, above a near-zero baseline, and remains roughly `r round(stats$ctrl_pctfloor/stats$neo_pctfloor)`-fold below the productive controls in detection rate.

Crucially, that marginal excess is not productive burden, and it is not bought by depth. Sequencing depth raised the odds of detecting *any* HPV read (OR per log₁₀ reads `r fo(stats$m2a_l10_or)`, `r oci(stats$m2a_l10_lo, stats$m2a_l10_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2a_l10_p)`), but it did not raise the odds of reaching the detection floor, either as a covariate across tiers (OR `r fo(stats$m2b_l10_or)`, `r oci(stats$m2b_l10_lo, stats$m2b_l10_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_l10_p)`) or within the neoplasia tier alone (OR `r fo(stats$neo_depth_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$neo_depth_lo, stats$neo_depth_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$neo_depth_p)`). The deepest cSCC/AK libraries, at `r p1(stats$neo_maxreads)`M reads, did not cross the productive floor. Consistent with a residual footprint rather than active infection, neoplasia showed a clear excess of *trace* HPV (any read; OR `r fo(stats$m2a_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$m2a_lo, stats$m2a_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2a_p)` vs unselected skin) alongside its small floor-level excess, but neither amounted to productive burden. The depth-matched detection profile confirms the same pattern non-parametrically: across every sequencing-depth bin, productive controls detect at 90–100% while neoplasia and unselected skin stay near zero (@suppfig-depth). At population scale, then, HPV in cutaneous neoplasia is a low-level, transcriptionally inactive trace, the signature predicted by the hit-and-run model, and not the productive infection seen in warts. That trace is also not integrated virus, which the junction analysis measures rather than infers: of `r stats$jx_neo_n` HPV-positive cSCC/AK libraries carrying enough viral reads to test, `r stats$jx_neo_epi` show no integration junction at all, and the `r stats$jx_neo_int` that do are HPV16 libraries the broadened query swept in from mucosal disease (@supptbl-cin), where integration is the expected state. The negatives are not limited by viral depth: integration was called in a library carrying only `r comma(stats$jx_pos_minreads)` HPV reads, and every junction-negative cSCC library exceeds that by at least `r formatC(stats$jx_neg_minfold, format="f", digits=1)`-fold.

Nor is it explained by how the libraries were built. Depth is one bound on viral-transcript recovery; RNA-selection chemistry is the other, and poly-A capture is the chemistry least favourable to it. Chemistry was resolved for `r comma(stats$chem_n)` libraries (`r pp(stats$chem_pct)`%) from SRA metadata and library-construction protocol text, and it is not balanced across tiers, but the imbalance runs against the negative result rather than producing it: the neoplasia tier is rRNA-depleted in `r pp(stats$chem_neo_ribo)`% of libraries against `r pp(stats$chem_skin_ribo)`% of unselected skin, while the productive controls, the tier in which productive infection is abundant, contain no rRNA-depleted libraries at all. The tier in which no productive infection is found was thus built, three times more often than its comparator, with the chemistry most favourable to finding it. Within the two tiers of the contrast, and adjusting for depth and tier, rRNA-depleted libraries were no more likely than poly-A libraries to carry any HPV read (OR `r fo(stats$chem_ribo_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$chem_ribo_lo, stats$chem_ribo_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$chem_ribo_p)`; OR `r fo(stats$chem_ribo_or_all)`, `r oci(stats$chem_ribo_lo_all, stats$chem_ribo_hi_all)` across all tiers). What did move trace detection, by three- to four-fold at equal depth, was not selection chemistry but amplification: SMART template-switching (OR `r fo(stats$chem_smart_or)`) and 3'-barcoded droplet libraries (OR `r fo(stats$chem_tenx_or)`), a pattern that reads as amplification and barcode-swapping artefact rather than recovery. Adding chemistry to the models leaves both contrasts intact (trace OR `r fo(stats$m2a_or_chem)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2a_p_chem)`; floor-level OR `r fo(stats$m2b_or_chem)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p_chem)`). The decisive test is to discard the ambiguity and use only the favourable chemistry: among the `r comma(stats$ribo_n)` rRNA-depleted libraries in the contrast (`r comma(stats$ribo_skin_n)` skin, `r stats$ribo_neo_n` neoplasia from `r stats$ribo_neo_studies` studies, median `r mreads(stats$ribo_neo_medreads)` and deepest `r mreads(stats$ribo_neo_maxreads)` reads), the trace excess in neoplasia is larger still (OR `r fo(stats$ribo_or)`, `r oci(stats$ribo_lo, stats$ribo_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$ribo_p)`) and not one library, in either tier, reached the productive floor.

Tissue that cannot host the virus fixes the meaning of that trace. Papillomaviruses replicate only in differentiating stratified squamous epithelium, so cutaneous adipose, blood and neural material offer no permissive compartment at all; the `r stats$npt_n` such libraries nonetheless carried a trace HPV read at `r pp(stats$npt_pctany)`%, indistinguishable from the `r pp(stats$uns_pctany)`% of unselected skin, while `r pp(stats$npt_pctfloor)`% reached the detection floor and not one yielded a single assignable HPV type. The background rate of trace HPV reads is therefore not a measure of infection: it is the assay's floor, reproduced at the same level in tissue where infection is biologically impossible. Read against that control, the trace signal in unselected skin and in neoplasia is what a library returns when no productive infection is present.

Most of the small floor-level excess is in fact attributable to a handful of libraries the broadened SCC/CIN query captured: `r stats$cin_n` of the `r stats$neo_pos_floor` above-floor neoplasia libraries are high-risk *mucosal* HPV16 cases in squamous-cell carcinoma, conservatively retained in the neoplasia tier (@supptbl-cin). Excluding them halves the effect, lowering cutaneous-neoplasia floor-level detection to `r pp(stats$neo_pctfloor_cut)`% (OR vs skin `r fo(stats$m2b_or_cut)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m2b_p_cut)`) and strengthening the productivity contrast against warts/EV (OR `r fo(stats$m3_or_cut)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m3_p_cut)`), so the retained tier is the conservative choice.

### The assay detects bona fide productive cutaneous HPV, including genuine infections in primary skin

That the trace neoplasia signal reflects biology rather than assay insensitivity is established by the positive controls, which the pipeline detects robustly. Among targeted wart/EV libraries, `r round(stats$m3_ctrl_pct)`% (`r stats$m3_ctrl_prod`/`r stats$m3_ctrl_n`) met the strict productive criterion (≥3 L1 major-capsid reads), spanning the classic cutaneous repertoire: wart-associated alpha types (HPV2, HPV27, HPV57), low-risk mucocutaneous types (HPV6, HPV11), and beta/gamma types (@supptbl-types). Productive infection was significantly more frequent in these controls than among HPV-positive neoplasia libraries (`r round(stats$m3_neo_pct)`%, `r stats$m3_neo_prod`/`r stats$m3_neo_n`; Fisher exact OR `r fo(stats$m3_or)`, 95% CI `r oci(stats$m3_lo, stats$m3_hi)`, *P* = `r fp(stats$m3_p)`).

Even so, a minority of genuine, non-cell-line skin lesions did harbour unambiguous productive infection, showing that the trace-level population result does not exclude real cutaneous HPV disease. The strongest cases were a cSCC skin library productively infected with the gamma-type HPV12 (99.8% genome coverage; L1 = 1,803, L2 = 3,546 reads), two HPV16-productive cSCC libraries, and two libraries from cutaneous actinic-keratosis/cSCC cohorts whose SRA records carry no tissue field (an actinic keratosis and a carcinoma) co-infected with the gamma types HPV96 and HPV182 at near-complete genome coverage (98–99%) and high depth (60–245×), with hundreds of L1 and L2 reads each (@supptbl-productive). These represent the answer to the productive-infection question: bona fide, high-confidence productive beta/gamma-HPV infections do occur in primary skin and skin-associated lesions, but they are the exception against a null background. They do not answer the non-traditional-tissue question, because the residual tier that would have to supply that evidence is defined by the *absence* of a site keyword rather than by an identified non-cutaneous site: the two co-infected libraries above sit there only because their cutaneous cohorts record no tissue field at all.

### The HPV type landscape is partitioned by population

The HPV-type-by-tier catalogue (@supptbl-types) recapitulates these conclusions in a single descriptive view, and the corrected tiering sharpens it. The high-risk mucosal types HPV16/HPV18 are confined almost entirely to cell-line material (`r ciA("HPV16","cell_line")` and `r ciA("HPV18","cell_line")` of cell-line libraries). Productive controls are dominated by cutaneous wart types (HPV57, HPV2, HPV27) plus the low-risk mucocutaneous HPV6/HPV11 and gamma types (HPV4, HPV-mKN1). The EV tier carries precisely the beta-types the syndrome is defined by (HPV9, HPV14, HPV20, HPV25, HPV47) alongside an alpha co-detection. Peri-lesional mucosa carries the mucosal alpha repertoire of its adjacent condylomata (HPV11 in `r ciA("HPV11","peri_lesional")` of libraries, HPV42, HPV6, HPV74, HPV90). Unselected skin, by contrast, contributes no HPV type at all above the two-library display threshold except two HPV18 contamination calls: its beta/gamma reservoir is real but sits entirely below the assignment threshold, and is recovered only at the detection tier (below). The genuine neoplasia-associated productive infections are the gamma/alpha types noted above (HPV12, HPV16, HPV96, HPV182). Collapsed from type to genus (@fig-genus), the same partition is a single picture: productive controls are alpha with a gamma minority, EV biopsies are essentially pure beta (`r kG("Beta","EV")` libraries), peri-lesional mucosa is purely alpha, cell lines are alpha, and unselected skin is flat and low across alpha, beta and gamma, with the study's only nu detections. Cutaneous neoplasia is the one tissue tier in which beta exceeds alpha (`r ciG("Beta","Neoplasia")` versus `r ciG("Alpha","Neoplasia")`), the genus-level shadow of a beta-HPV footprint. The epidemiological reservoir of cutaneous beta/gamma HPV in healthy skin is therefore real but transcriptionally quiet, productive disease is the property of warts and EV, and HPV-associated cutaneous neoplasia carries the virus, when at all, as a trace, non-productive footprint.

Extending this catalogue below the assignment threshold answers the descriptive question of *which* types make up the trace. A detection-tier re-map of the HPV-positive but untyped libraries, taking the best-hit reference from unique alignments at sub-threshold coverage, resolved a confident low-coverage type for `r stats$trace_resolved` of `r stats$trace_n` such libraries across `r stats$trace_ntypes` types (@supptbl-trace). This recovers the expected commensal signal at the sensitivity floor: healthy skin carried a diverse cutaneous reservoir (`r stats$trace_skin_cut` of `r stats$trace_skin_n` resolved skin calls were beta-, gamma- or nu-types, including HPV12/HPV20, HPV4/HPV65/HPV134 and candidate skin-virome types), cutaneous neoplasia the carcinoma-associated beta and gamma types (HPV5, HPV12, HPV182, HPV222), while the mucosal HPV16/HPV18 signal stayed confined to cell-line material and a low-level contamination overlay. These are low-coverage, non-productive detections that identify the type without bearing on productivity, and so extend the type catalogue rather than qualify the trace-not-productive conclusion.

A further descriptive feature of the catalogue is that types frequently co-occur: `r cf$libs` of the `r cf$typed` typed libraries carry two or more assigned references, up to five in one library (@supptbl-coinf). Because coverage is scored from uniquely-mapped reads alone, cross-mapping between similar types cannot generate these calls. The commonest pairing by far is HPV11 with HPV42, which co-occur in `r cf$both1142` libraries, while only `r cf$only42` carry HPV42 without HPV11; in the peri-lesional tier the pairing is forced by the marginal counts of @supptbl-types (14 HPV11 and 13 HPV42 calls over 15 libraries). We nonetheless present this as a hypothesis rather than a finding, for three reasons set out in @supptbl-coinf. The co-infected libraries are heavily pseudo-replicated, `r cf$pair_libs` of the `r cf$libs` coming from `r cf$pair_donors` donors of one study, each sequenced in three fractions across two SRA submissions; the secondary type in a co-infection is usually near the detection threshold (median depth `r p1(cf$sec_med_depth)`×, `r cf$sec_shallow`% below 5×), to the point that one donor's MeRIP input and IP fractions call different second types; and requiring both partners to clear a stricter coverage bar leaves only `r cf$strict_libs` HPV11/HPV42 libraries from `r cf$strict_donors` donors. Within that stricter set the deeper type differs by tissue, HPV11 in the condyloma lesion and HPV42 in the two peri-lesional specimens, but HPV42 clears the bar only where it is abundant, so tissue tropism and detection sensitivity are confounded. The pattern is worth testing in a cohort assembled for the purpose; it cannot be resolved here.


::: {#fig-genus}
![](figure3.png)

HPV genus prevalence by population tier. The two type catalogues are collapsed from HPV type to HPV genus: the assigned-type catalogue of @supptbl-types (top row), the detection-tier trace catalogue of @supptbl-trace (middle row), and their union (bottom row), a library contributing to at most one of the first two rows. Points are Beta-Binomial posterior means with 95% credible intervals (Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior), computed exactly as in the two tables so that a cell here and the corresponding table cell quote the same prevalence; the number above each point is the count of libraries detected, and the denominator is the tier size (Methods). Grey crosses mark tiers in which a genus was never detected; they sit at the axis floor because the *y*-axis is log-scaled and the lowest tick, labelled 0, is a placeholder for zero. A library carrying two types of different genera contributes to both, so the points within a tier need not sum to that tier's positivity rate. Read across the bottom row, the figure is the type landscape of the study in one panel: the productive controls are alpha-dominated (`r kG("Alpha","Productive controls")` libraries, `r ciG("Alpha","Productive controls")`) with a gamma minority (`r ciG("Gamma","Productive controls")`) and no beta at all, the repertoire of cutaneous and mucocutaneous warts; the EV biopsies are the mirror image, essentially pure beta (`r kG("Beta","EV")`, `r ciG("Beta","EV")`), the genus the syndrome is defined by; peri-lesional mucosa is purely alpha (`r kG("Alpha","Peri-lesional mucosa")`), carrying its adjacent condylomata's types and nothing cutaneous; cell lines are alpha (`r ciG("Alpha","Cell line")`), the integrated HPV16/HPV18 contamination signature; unselected skin is flat and low, with alpha, beta and gamma at indistinguishable rates near `r ciG("Beta","Unselected skin")` and the study's only nu detections (`r kG("Nu","Unselected skin")` libraries, HPV41), the profile of a sparse commensal reservoir rather than of any one disease; and cutaneous neoplasia is the one tissue tier in which beta exceeds alpha (`r ciG("Beta","Neoplasia")` versus `r ciG("Alpha","Neoplasia")`), consistent with a beta-HPV footprint, though at prevalences one to two orders of magnitude below the productive tiers. The mu genus (HPV1, the classic plantar-wart type) was detected in no tier.
:::

### A Bayesian re-analysis under weakly-informative priors confirms the contrasts

To confirm these conclusions are not artefacts of the frequentist framework or of the near-complete separation in the strongest contrast, we refitted the positivity, depth-controlled detection and productivity models as Bayesian logistic regressions under weakly-informative priors (Normal(0, 2.5) on the log-odds coefficients; Methods), summarising each effect by its posterior median odds ratio, 95% credible interval (CrI) and posterior probability of direction (@supptbl-bayes). The contamination enrichment and the trace excess were reproduced essentially unchanged and with near-certainty (cell-line OR `r bor(bget("M1_cell_line"))`, engineered OR `r bor(bget("M1_engineered"))`, neoplasia trace OR `r bor(bget("M2a_neoplasia_vs_skin_any"))`; each with P(OR > 1) > 0.999). Crucially, the productive-controls-versus-skin contrast, whose frequentist odds ratio (`r fo(stats$fish_or)`) is inflated and unstable under separation, regularised to a finite but still enormous posterior OR of `r bor(bget("M2c_controls_vs_skin_floor"))` (`r bor(bget("M2c_controls_vs_skin_floor_studentt"))` under a heavier-tailed Student-*t* prior): the productive gap between warts/EV and skin is real, not a separation artefact. Deeper sequencing within neoplasia again bought no productive-level detection (OR `r bor(bget("M2d_depth_within_neoplasia"))`, P(OR > 1) = `r pdir(bget("M2d_depth_within_neoplasia")$p_gt1)`), and the warts/EV-versus-neoplasia productivity contrast held (OR `r bor(bget("M3_controls_vs_neoplasia"))`, P(OR > 1) = `r pdir(bget("M3_controls_vs_neoplasia")$p_gt1)`). The neoplasia-versus-skin comparison at floor level, whose frequentist interval is wide because it rests on `r stats$neo_pos_floor` above-floor libraries, shrinks under the prior but stays clearly positive (OR `r bor(bget("M2b_neoplasia_vs_skin_floor"))`, P(OR > 1) = `r pdir(bget("M2b_neoplasia_vs_skin_floor")$p_gt1)`): the small floor-level elevation of neoplasia over clean skin is genuine. It is nonetheless negligible beside the near-four-orders-of-magnitude productive-control effect, and it does not alter the trace-not-productive conclusion.
